docs.title: Working with architects
docs.text: For service designers, interaction designers, content designers and user researchers: when to involve an architect, what to bring, and what you can expect in return.

docs.title: Why this matters to designers and researchers
docs.text:
Many decisions that shape the user experience are architecture decisions too. They are cheap to change in discovery and alpha, and expensive afterwards. For example:

  • Sign-in and acting on behalf of others - who can do what for which business or holding. See acting on behalf of an organisation or holding.
  • A forms platform or a bespoke front end - what you can design depends on the choice. See GR-FE-04.
  • Processing in the background - whether users get an answer straight away or a reference number and an email later. See asynchronous submission.
  • Uploading files - what users wait for while files are checked, and what happens when one is rejected. See file upload with malware scanning.
  • Working offline - what field users can do without a signal. See field working and devices.
  • AI - what users are told, and how they challenge a decision. See GR-AI-03 and GR-AI-04.

If you design or research any of these, involve an architect early. The guardrails each role leads are on the pages for service designers, interaction designers, content designers and user researchers.

docs.title: When to involve an architect, and what to bring
docs.text: This page covers the architecture touchpoints only. For your own discipline, use the Defra Digital Service Manual: design, user research and content design, including what content designers do in discovery, alpha, beta and live.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Bring:

  • the current journey, mapped against the systems, teams and organisations behind each step
  • the information you ask users for, so an architect can tell you what Defra already holds and where the authoritative sources are (GR-DATA-02, GR-DATA-04)
  • what you are learning about users' devices, connectivity and who acts for whom

docs.title: Alpha
docs.text:
Bring:

  • your riskiest assumptions on the user side, so you can test them alongside the riskiest technical assumptions rather than separately
  • the prototypes that depend on a technical choice, such as sign-in, file upload or a forms platform - prototype these on the real platforms where it matters, so research tests what users will actually get
  • anything that would mean departing from the GOV.UK Design System

docs.title: Beta
docs.text:
Bring:

  • what users see when a dependency is slow or fails, such as a payment provider or a back-office system, and the content for it (GR-OPS-04)
  • confirmation and status content: what happens next, how long it takes and how users find out - based on how long processing really takes
  • findings from research with assistive technology users that need a technical fix

docs.title: Live
docs.text:
Bring:

  • how you will tell users about incidents and planned downtime, and who sends those messages
  • research findings that point to a change in how the service works, not just how it looks - these may be a significant change

docs.title: What architects do in return
docs.text:
Architects working with your team should:

  • come to show and tells and research playbacks, so they hear from users directly
  • join design critiques for journeys with technical constraints, such as sign-in, payments or file upload
  • record decisions that affect the user experience as ADRs, with the designer or researcher named as a contributor, so the reasons are kept alongside the technical ones - see architecture decision records
  • explain constraints in plain English, and say which ones are fixed and which can be challenged
  • raise it early when a technical decision will change what users see

docs.title: How to ask
docs.text:
• If your team has an architect, talk to them first.
  • If not, contact the Delivery Architecture team at delivery.architecture@defra.gov.uk. They will tell you the principal architect for your delivery group. See architecture in the Defra Digital Service Manual.
  • You can also use the routes on the architecture team page, which describes the architecture drop-in sessions.

To be confirmed

docs.title: Artefacts
docs.text:
• Architecture decision record (ADR) log - Record hosting, identity, integration and data decisions.
  • C4 system context diagram - Confirm the context.
  • C4 container diagram - Draw the containers for the options you are testing.
  • Threat model - Run the first collaborative threat model.
  • Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) - Complete the DPIA if you process personal data.
  • Service tier - Agree the tier with the service owner.
  • Non-functional requirements (NFRs) - Choose NFRs from the catalogue for your tier.
  • Exit plan - Draft an exit plan for each new product or supplier.

docs.title: Must guardrails
docs.text:
• GR-AI-02 Use approved AI services and tenancies - AI services chosen for the design, each confirmed as running in a Defra tenancy or under an approved agreement
  • GR-AI-03 Keep a human accountable - Design of the human oversight and challenge route for decisions with significant effects, tested with users in prototypes
  • GR-API-07 Secure every API - Authentication, authorisation, input validation and rate limiting designed for each API
  • GR-TECH-01 Look for something to reuse first - ADR recording the reuse options considered and why they did or did not fit
  • GR-TECH-04 Assess SaaS before you adopt it - Security, data protection, data location, accessibility and single sign-on assessed before contract
  • GR-DATA-06 Protect personal data by design - Draft DPIA, with data minimisation and retention designed in
  • GR-FE-01 Meet WCAG 2.2 AA - Prototypes built with accessible components, and a plan for an accessibility audit and assistive technology testing
  • GR-FE-02 Use the GOV.UK Design System - Prototypes built with the GOV.UK Design System, with departures recorded and researched
  • GR-FE-06 Support Welsh where required - Whether the Welsh Language Standards apply decided, and the service designed for translation
  • GR-HOST-01 Use Defra's strategic delivery platform by default - The design runs on the Core Delivery Platform, or an exception has been requested
  • GR-IAM-01 Use the strategic customer identity services - Sign-in designed with Defra Customer Identity, and tested with users
  • GR-IAM-05 No secrets in code - Secret scanning on from the first commit, and secrets held in a managed store from the start
  • GR-OPEN-01 Code in the open - Code public in a Defra GitHub organisation from the first commit, or a recorded reason for keeping a repository private
  • GR-SEC-01 Follow Secure by Design - Secure by Design activities for alpha completed, including security requirements in the backlog
  • GR-SEC-02 Keep a current threat model - First threat model, created by the team
  • GR-SEC-03 Classify information - Controls in the design that match the classification
  • GR-SEC-09 Manage risk explicitly - Risks from controls that cannot be met recorded, with an owner
  • GR-DEV-02 All code in Defra source control - All code, including prototypes and infrastructure code written by suppliers, in a Defra-owned GitHub organisation from the first commit

docs.title: Should guardrails
docs.text:
• GR-AI-01 Consider AI first - ADR recording the AI options considered and why they were or were not used
  • GR-AI-05 Evaluate, monitor and threat model - Evaluation plan for accuracy, bias and safety, and AI-specific threats in the threat model
  • GR-AI-06 Talk to the TDA about novel use - Technical Design Authority review outcome recorded in the ADR
  • GR-AI-07 Suppliers use AI coding assistants openly and safely - Supplier's agreed list of AI coding assistants and how each runs within Defra-approved terms, the review process for generated code, and disclosure in pull requests or delivery reports
  • GR-AI-08 Give agents the least privilege they need - Each agent's tools and permissions listed in the design, with a workload identity for the agent
  • GR-AI-09 Get human approval for consequential actions - Agent actions classified, and the actions that need human approval identified in the design
  • GR-AI-11 Defend agents against prompt injection - Threat model covering prompt injection through every input the agent reads
  • GR-API-01 API first - API specification written before or alongside the user interface
  • GR-API-02 Describe APIs with open specifications - Draft OpenAPI 3 or AsyncAPI documents for the interfaces you are prototyping
  • GR-API-03 Follow government API standards - API design reviewed against the GDS API technical and data standards
  • GR-API-05 No integration through shared databases - Container diagram showing integration only through APIs, events or governed data products
  • GR-API-06 Use events for change notifications - Event and message definitions described in AsyncAPI
  • GR-TECH-02 Buy commodity, build differentiating - Buy or build options appraisal in the ADR or business case
  • GR-TECH-03 Plan your exit before you enter - Draft exit plan for each new product, platform or significant supplier
  • GR-TECH-05 Prefer open standards and portable technology - ADR noting the open standards used and how portable the choice is
  • GR-DATA-01 Every data set has an owner - Each data set the service will create or hold identified, with a proposed information asset owner
  • GR-DATA-02 Use authoritative sources - Data flow diagram naming the authoritative source for each shared entity, and how any copies are refreshed
  • GR-DATA-03 Use agreed data standards and identifiers - Data model using the agreed data standards and identifiers
  • GR-DATA-04 Collect once, share safely - Journey design showing users are not asked for information Defra already holds, and data sharing agreements where required
  • GR-DATA-10 Handle research data safely - The same for alpha research, with DPIA screening done for the research and any new research tool assessed
  • GR-DATA-11 No real personal data in prototypes - Prototypes and research materials use made-up data, including data a participant types in during a session
  • GR-DIG-01 Challenge paper and manual processes - Discovery findings showing paper, email and manual steps in the current process and how the new design removes or justifies each one
  • GR-DIG-02 Design across organisational boundaries - A map of the whole service, including the parts other teams and organisations deliver, and agreed hand-offs between them
  • GR-DIG-03 Provide assisted digital and offline routes - Assisted digital and offline routes designed and tested with users who need them
  • GR-FIELD-01 Choose devices that suit the job - User research on the working environment, and the device choice recorded in an ADR
  • GR-FIELD-02 Design field tools to work offline - Field journeys tested with no connection, including sync after reconnecting and conflict handling
  • GR-FIELD-03 Manage and secure every device - Device management approach agreed for the devices the service will use
  • GR-FE-03 Progressive enhancement - Core journeys tested with JavaScript turned off
  • GR-FE-04 Consider forms platforms first - ADR noting whether the forms capability was considered
  • GR-FE-05 Design for low bandwidth and rural users - Page weight budget, save-progress design and testing on slow connections
  • GR-FE-07 Tell users what is happening when things fail or are slow - Each dependency that can fail or be slow identified with the developers, and what users see in each case designed and tested in the prototype
  • GR-HOST-02 Public cloud first - Where the platform cannot be used, the hosting design uses a Defra-managed public cloud tenancy
  • GR-HOST-04 Use managed services before self-managed - Hosting design listing the managed services used
  • GR-HOST-05 Consistent, disposable environments - Environments created from the same code, and how lower environments avoid real personal data
  • GR-HOST-06 Host data in the UK - Hosting design places every data store and backup in UK regions
  • GR-HOST-07 Design for the resilience the service needs - Recovery time and recovery point objectives agreed with the service owner, and a design that meets them
  • GR-IAM-04 Separate authentication from authorisation - Authorisation rules written down and covered by automated tests
  • GR-OPEN-02 Licence clearly - LICENCE file in every repository from the start
  • GR-OPEN-03 Publish safely - Secret scanning and push protection on for every repository from the first commit
  • GR-OPEN-04 Reuse and contribute back - Reuse and upstream contributions noted in ADRs and pull requests
  • GR-PROD-01 Fund and run products, not projects - A named, long-lived team responsible for the product, with a roadmap beyond the current funding period
  • GR-PROD-02 Name the product owner and service owner - Named product owner and service owner, recorded in the service catalogue
  • GR-PROD-03 Contribute to platforms rather than working around them - Requests and contributions raised with platform teams, and ADRs where the team worked around a platform
  • GR-SEC-08 Protect the supply chain - Security assessment of suppliers and third-party products in the design
  • GR-DEV-01 Use the supported languages and frameworks - ADR recording the reason wherever the service uses a different stack
  • GR-DEV-03 Protect the main branch - Main branch protected from the start, with changes through reviewed pull requests
  • GR-DEV-05 Automated testing at the right levels - Test results from the pipeline at each level
  • GR-DEV-07 Follow shared coding standards - Linting and formatting checks in the pipeline
  • GR-DEV-08 Document as you go - README explaining what the service does and how to run, test and deploy it, with links to its ADRs
  • GR-DEV-09 Record significant decisions as ADRs - ADR log in the repository or linked from its README
  • GR-SUS-01 Consider sustainability in design decisions - Environmental impact recorded in ADRs for hosting and technology choices
  • GR-SUS-04 Keep data and pages lean - Data retention settings and page weight measurements

docs.title: Could guardrails
docs.text:
• GR-FIELD-04 Check connectivity before you design - Connectivity in the places the service will be used checked, and the approach recorded
  • GR-OPEN-05 Blog and show the thing - Blog posts, show and tells or contributions to this site
  • GR-SUS-03 Choose lower-carbon regions and services - Region and service choice recorded with its carbon intensity

docs.title: Artefacts
docs.text:

docs.title: Must guardrails
docs.text:
• GR-AI-02 Use approved AI services and tenancies - The AI services in the built service run only in approved tenancies, shown in the hosting design and configuration
  • GR-AI-03 Keep a human accountable - Human review and challenge built into the service and tested with users and staff
  • GR-AI-04 Be transparent - Draft Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard record, and the notice telling users about AI tested with them
  • GR-API-07 Secure every API - These controls built and covered by security testing
  • GR-DATA-06 Protect personal data by design - Approved DPIA, and retention and deletion built and tested
  • GR-DATA-09 Retain and dispose of records properly - Retention schedule identified for each type of record, and disposal built in
  • GR-FE-01 Meet WCAG 2.2 AA - Accessibility audit and assistive technology testing completed, issues fixed, and an accessibility statement published
  • GR-FE-02 Use the GOV.UK Design System - The service uses GOV.UK Frontend, with design decisions recording any departures
  • GR-FE-06 Support Welsh where required - Welsh content and journeys built and tested where the standards apply
  • GR-HOST-01 Use Defra's strategic delivery platform by default - The service runs on the Core Delivery Platform, or under an approved exception
  • GR-IAM-01 Use the strategic customer identity services - Integration with Defra Customer Identity built and tested
  • GR-IAM-02 Staff sign in with Microsoft Entra ID - Staff sign in through Microsoft Entra ID with multi-factor authentication, and there are no local staff accounts
  • GR-IAM-03 Authorise on least privilege - Role and group model built, with users, services and pipelines given only the permissions they need
  • GR-IAM-05 No secrets in code - All secrets in a managed store with rotation, using workload identity where possible
  • GR-IAM-06 Privileged access is controlled and audited - Just-in-time privileged access with phishing-resistant MFA configured, and logged to the security operations centre
  • GR-OPS-05 Be ready for live before you go live - Before public beta, the support model, on-call arrangements, runbooks, incident process and live owner agreed, and the service catalogue entry made
  • GR-OPEN-01 Code in the open - Repositories public, or the reasons for keeping them private reviewed
  • GR-SEC-01 Follow Secure by Design - Secure by Design activities for beta completed, including controls built and tested
  • GR-SEC-02 Keep a current threat model - Threat model updated as controls are built and tested
  • GR-SEC-04 Encrypt in transit and at rest - TLS 1.2 or higher for all traffic and encryption at rest for every data store, confirmed as built
  • GR-SEC-05 Scan continuously and fix quickly - Static analysis, dependency, container and infrastructure scanning running in the pipeline
  • GR-SEC-06 Test before go-live and after major change - IT health check before go-live, and a remediation tracker
  • GR-SEC-07 Log for detection and response - Authentication, authorisation failures, administrative actions and data exports sent to the security operations centre, and tested
  • GR-SEC-09 Manage risk explicitly - Residual risks accepted by the right owner through the security exception process, each with an expiry date
  • GR-DEV-02 All code in Defra source control - All source, infrastructure and pipeline code in the Defra GitHub organisation, with nothing held only by a supplier

docs.title: Should guardrails
docs.text:
• GR-AI-05 Evaluate, monitor and threat model - Evaluation results for accuracy, bias and safety before release, and mitigations for AI threats tested
  • GR-AI-07 Suppliers use AI coding assistants openly and safely - Supplier's agreed list of AI coding assistants and how each runs within Defra-approved terms, the review process for generated code, and disclosure in pull requests or delivery reports
  • GR-AI-08 Give agents the least privilege they need - Agent permissions configured as designed and tested, including that the agent cannot reach tools it should not

  • GR-AI-11 Defend agents against prompt injection - Prompt injection mitigations tested, including attempts to misuse tools and leak data
  • GR-API-01 API first - API specification written before or alongside the user interface

  • GR-API-06 Use events for change notifications - Event and message definitions described in AsyncAPI
  • GR-API-08 Make APIs discoverable - Entry in the platform API catalogue
  • GR-TECH-03 Plan your exit before you enter - Exit plan agreed, with contracts giving Defra its data and the right to export it in open formats
  • GR-DATA-01 Every data set has an owner - Information asset register entries with a named owner for each data set
  • GR-DATA-02 Use authoritative sources - The service reads from the authoritative sources as designed, tested with the source owners
  • GR-DATA-03 Use agreed data standards and identifiers - Data stored and exchanged using the agreed standards, checked in testing
  • GR-DATA-04 Collect once, share safely - Journey design showing users are not asked for information Defra already holds, and data sharing agreements where required
  • GR-DATA-05 Describe your data - Published metadata records in UK GEMINI or DCAT
  • GR-DATA-07 Open by default - Link to the published open data and its licence
  • GR-DATA-08 Manage data quality - Data quality measures and regular reports
  • GR-DATA-10 Handle research data safely - Research data from earlier phases deleted on schedule, and the same controls for beta research
  • GR-DATA-11 No real personal data in prototypes - Test and research environments use synthetic or anonymised data; any exception agreed through a DPIA
  • GR-DIG-02 Design across organisational boundaries - A map of the whole service, including the parts other teams and organisations deliver, and agreed hand-offs between them
  • GR-DIG-03 Provide assisted digital and offline routes - Assisted digital and offline routes designed and tested with users who need them
  • GR-FIELD-02 Design field tools to work offline - Field journeys tested with no connection, including sync after reconnecting and conflict handling
  • GR-FIELD-03 Manage and secure every device - Devices enrolled in Defra device management, with encryption, patching, screen lock and remote wipe confirmed
  • GR-FE-03 Progressive enhancement - Core journeys tested with JavaScript turned off
  • GR-FE-05 Design for low bandwidth and rural users - Page weight budget, save-progress design and testing on slow connections
  • GR-FE-07 Tell users what is happening when things fail or are slow - The front end shows the designed content when a dependency fails or is slow, tested by switching dependencies off
  • GR-HOST-02 Public cloud first - The service runs in a Defra-managed public cloud tenancy
  • GR-HOST-03 Everything as code - Infrastructure, configuration and pipelines defined as code in the repository, with no manual changes to production
  • GR-HOST-04 Use managed services before self-managed - Hosting design listing the managed services used
  • GR-HOST-05 Consistent, disposable environments - Environments created from the same code, and how lower environments avoid real personal data
  • GR-HOST-06 Host data in the UK - Data location confirmed for every data store and backup as built
  • GR-HOST-07 Design for the resilience the service needs - Multi-zone design built, and recovery tested before go-live
  • GR-IAM-04 Separate authentication from authorisation - Authorisation rules written down and covered by automated tests
  • GR-OPS-01 Use the platform's observability tooling - Logs, metrics and traces reaching the platform's observability tooling, and security events reaching the security operations centre
  • GR-OPS-02 Log in a structured, safe way - Structured logs with correlation identifiers, tested to show no secrets or unnecessary personal data are logged
  • GR-OPS-03 Define and measure service levels - Agreed service level objectives with monitoring and alerts
  • GR-OPS-04 Health checks and graceful degradation - Health endpoints, timeout and retry settings, and a design for when dependencies fail
  • GR-OPS-07 Measure performance and cost - Published key performance indicators and cost tags on cloud resources
  • GR-OPEN-02 Licence clearly - LICENCE file with the Open Government Licence or MIT licence in every repository
  • GR-OPEN-03 Publish safely - Secret scanning and push protection on for every repository
  • GR-OPEN-04 Reuse and contribute back - Reuse and upstream contributions noted in ADRs and pull requests

  • GR-PROD-02 Name the product owner and service owner - Named product owner and service owner, recorded in the service catalogue
  • GR-PROD-03 Contribute to platforms rather than working around them - Requests and contributions raised with platform teams, and ADRs where the team worked around a platform
  • GR-SEC-08 Protect the supply chain - Dependencies pinned and verified, and a software bill of materials produced in the pipeline

  • GR-DEV-04 Continuous integration and delivery - Every change built, tested, scanned and deployed by an automated pipeline, with rollback tested
  • GR-DEV-05 Automated testing at the right levels - Test results from the pipeline at each level
  • GR-DEV-06 Manage dependencies actively - Dependabot or Renovate configured, software composition analysis in the pipeline, and runtimes on supported versions
  • GR-DEV-07 Follow shared coding standards - Linting and formatting checks in the pipeline
  • GR-DEV-08 Document as you go - README explaining what the service does and how to run, test and deploy it, with links to its ADRs
  • GR-DEV-09 Record significant decisions as ADRs - ADR log in the repository or linked from its README
  • GR-SUS-02 Right-size and switch off - Autoscaling and out-of-hours schedules for non-production environments
  • GR-SUS-04 Keep data and pages lean - Data retention settings and page weight measurements

docs.title: Patterns that help
docs.text:
• Acting on behalf of an organisation or holding - Users act for a business, a land holding or another person, and the service must check they are allowed to.
  • Reading from an authoritative source - A service needs shared data - customers, organisations, holdings, locations or species - that another part of Defra owns.
  • File upload with malware scanning - Users upload documents or images, and the files must be scanned and stored safely before anyone opens them.
  • Publishing open data with metadata - You hold non-personal data that others could use, and want to publish it so it can be found, trusted and reused.

docs.title: Patterns that help
docs.text:
• Acting on behalf of an organisation or holding - Users act for a business, a land holding or another person, and the service must check they are allowed to.
  • Asynchronous submission with an outbox - A user submits something that other systems must process, and you do not want those systems' availability to block the user.
  • Reading from an authoritative source - A service needs shared data - customers, organisations, holdings, locations or species - that another part of Defra owns.
  • File upload with malware scanning - Users upload documents or images, and the files must be scanned and stored safely before anyone opens them.

docs.title: Working with architects
docs.text:
• Add the guardrail check to your repository on day one.
  • Raise anything that would need an exception early, with an ADR.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Light-touch, proportionate and as delegated as possible. Our governance exists to help teams make good decisions quickly, not to slow them down.

docs.title: Our approach
docs.text:
• Delegate by default. Most decisions should be made by delivery teams and their solution design authority. Central boards look only at what genuinely needs them.
  • Guardrails earn autonomy. The closer a design is to the guardrails and the handrail, the less governance it needs.
  • Engage early, not at the end. A 30-minute conversation in discovery saves weeks of rework at a gate.
  • Decide in the open. Decisions are recorded as ADRs, published wherever possible, and reusable by other teams.
  • Proportionate to risk. The route depends on novelty, reach and risk - not on the size of the team or the supplier.

docs.title: Seek advice, not permission
docs.text:
Most architecture decisions do not need a board. They need the right conversation at the right time. Before making a significant decision, a team:

  1. Asks for advice from the people with relevant expertise - an architect, the platform team, security - and from the people who will be affected by it.
  2. Decides - the team remains accountable for the decision and its outcome.
  3. Records the decision and the advice it received as an ADR, in the open.

This keeps decisions close to the work and fast enough to learn from, while making sure no one is surprised. It reflects the DDTS doctrine - teams decide without escalating every choice - and the government lightweight architecture approach. The boards below are for the minority of decisions that are novel, cross-cutting or outside the guardrails.

docs.title: How this relates to other assurance
docs.text:
Architecture governance works alongside, not instead of:

  • Service assessments against the Service Standard - see service assessments in the Defra Digital Service Manual
  • Operational service readiness, including the operational service design review board at the start of beta - see operational service readiness
  • Spend control under the Portfolio Assurance Board (PAB)
  • Security assurance through Secure by Design
  • Data protection through DPIAs and the Data Protection Officer
  • Investment approvals through the department's business case process (InvestCo)

Delivery groups have their own governance model, in which principal architects set the technology guardrails for the group in line with the enterprise architecture principles. The Delivery Architecture team handles exceptions to the Defra software development standards - see architecture in the Defra Digital Service Manual.

The TGB agrees strategies, the TDA is the technical decision-making authority, and in each solution design authority the principal architect is accountable for decisions within a roadmap agreed at the TDA. How exceptions on this site relate to the Delivery Architecture team's is still being agreed.

We aim to reuse evidence across these: an ADR log, threat model and architecture diagram prepared for one should satisfy the others.

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text: An architecture decision record (ADR) captures one significant decision, its context and its consequences. ADRs are how we make governance light: a decision that is written down well rarely needs a meeting.

docs.title: What to record
docs.text:
Record a decision when it:

  • is hard or expensive to reverse
  • departs from a guardrail or reference architecture
  • affects other teams, services or users
  • chooses between real options (technology, pattern, supplier, hosting)
  • someone in a year's time will ask "why did they do it this way?"

You do not need an ADR for routine implementation choices.

docs.title: Where to keep them
docs.text:
Where an ADR lives depends on who makes the decision.

Decision Made by Where it is kept A decision about one service or product The team, or its solution design authority (SDA) In the service repository, in docs/adr/ A decision that affects other teams, departs from a guardrail or sets direction for Defra The Technical Design Authority (TDA) or the Technology Governance Board (TGB) In the architecture decision register, a SharePoint list on the Defra architecture SharePoint site

docs.title: Team decisions: in your repository
docs.text: Keep ADRs as Markdown in your service repository, in docs/adr/, numbered in order (0001-use-defra-id-for-sign-in.md). They then live with the code, are reviewed through pull requests and are public by default (GR-OPEN-01).

docs.title: Enterprise decisions: in the architecture decision register
docs.text:
Decisions taken by the TDA and TGB are recorded in the architecture decision register, in the Defra Microsoft 365 tenancy. Keeping them there means they are under Defra's records management, can include information that should not be public, and do not depend on access to any one repository.

To be confirmed

docs.title: Raise a decision for review
docs.text:
If your decision needs the TDA or TGB, send it to them by email. You do not need a GitHub account or access to the SharePoint site.

  1. Write the decision using the ADR template, with status Proposed. For a TDA item, also complete the TDA submission template.
  2. Email it to StrategicEnterpriseArchitecture@defra.gov.uk, with "ADR:" and the decision title as the subject.
  3. An automated flow adds it to the register as Proposed and tells the architecture team.
  4. An architect triages it: it goes to the TDA, to the TGB, or back to your team or SDA if it does not need either.
  5. When the decision is made, the register is updated to Accepted or Rejected, with the date and any conditions, and you are told the outcome. Copy the outcome into your own repository's ADR if you keep one.

To be confirmed

docs.title: How to write a good ADR
docs.text:
• One decision per record. Short is good - a page is usually enough.
  • Make the context clear for someone who was not in the room.
  • Show real options, including the strategic option from the handrail.
  • Reference guardrail and capability ids (for example GR-HOST-01, BC05, TC08) so decisions can be searched across Defra.
  • Be honest about consequences, including the downsides.
  • Never edit an accepted ADR's decision. Supersede it with a new one and link the two.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
An ADR starts as Proposed. It becomes Accepted when the team, SDA or TDA agrees it, or Rejected. An accepted ADR is later Superseded by a newer ADR, or Deprecated when it no longer applies.

    Proposed --> Rejected
    Accepted --> Superseded: replaced by a newer ADR

docs.title: Exceptions to guardrails
docs.text:
Guardrails are defaults, and sometimes the right answer is different. The exception process gives you a quick, recorded decision - and tells us when a guardrail needs to change.

docs.title: Exceptions to the software development standards
docs.text:
The Defra software development standards are mandatory, and the Delivery Architecture team handles exceptions to them through its own governance process - see software development in the Defra Digital Service Manual. Some guardrails, such as GR-DEV-01 and GR-HOST-01, cover the same ground.

To be confirmed

TODO: how an exception to a Must guardrail agreed at the Technical Design Authority relates to the Delivery Architecture team's exception process for the software development standards - whether one request can cover both, and which comes first.

docs.title: What a good exception request includes
docs.text:
• The guardrail id and what you propose instead
  • Why the guardrail cannot be met - the user, business, technical or commercial reason
  • The risks of the exception and how you will manage them
  • How long the exception is needed, and what would let you return to the guardrail
  • The cost of meeting the guardrail, if that is the reason

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Time-limited. Exceptions have an expiry date, normally no more than 12 months, and are reviewed before renewal.
  • Recorded in the open. The exception register is published, except for security-sensitive details.
  • Quick. The TDA aims to decide within 10 working days of a complete request. Urgent requests can be handled out of cycle by the chair.
  • Feedback loop. Every quarter, the architecture team reviews exceptions. Where several teams need the same one, we propose a guardrail change to the TGB.

docs.title: Guardrails health
docs.text:

docs.title: Solution design authorities (SDAs)
docs.text:
SDAs are where most architecture decisions are assured. They sit close to delivery, within delivery groups or portfolios, with authority delegated from the TDA. In an SDA, the principal architect is accountable for decisions.

Draft - to be confirmed

Parts of this page, such as names, timings and thresholds, are still being confirmed by the architecture team. Use it as a guide, and check with your solution design authority before relying on the detail.

docs.title: Why delegate
docs.text: Central boards cannot know every service well, and every hand-off adds delay. SDAs know the domain, the users and the legacy estate. Delegating to them makes governance faster and better informed - as long as they work to the same guardrails.

docs.title: What an SDA can decide
docs.text:
• Designs that stay inside the guardrails and align with a roadmap agreed at the TDA
  • Departures from Should guardrails, recorded as ADRs
  • Technology choices within the supported stack
  • Architecture readiness for service assessments and phase gates

docs.title: What an SDA must escalate to the TDA
docs.text:
• Exceptions to Must guardrails
  • Novel or cross-cutting work (see triage)
  • Anything outside the delegation agreed for that SDA
  • Repeated deviations that suggest a guardrail should change

docs.title: Setting up an SDA
docs.text:
A delivery group or portfolio can request delegated authority from the TDA. It needs:

  1. A named principal architect accountable for decisions.
  2. A terms of reference stating its scope (which services and business capabilities) using the SDA terms of reference outline below.
  3. A public ADR log - or an internal one where publishing is not appropriate - that the TDA can see.
  4. Agreement to report a short summary of decisions and deviations to the TDA every quarter.

Delegation is reviewed annually. An SDA that works well may have its scope widened.

docs.title: Delivery groups and principal architects
docs.text:
Defra delivery groups have their own governance model, in which principal architects set the technology guardrails for the group in line with the enterprise architecture principles. The Delivery Architecture team tells each team who the principal architect for their delivery group is - see architecture in the Defra Digital Service Manual.

How the three levels fit together:

  • The Technology Governance Board (TGB) agrees strategies.
  • The Technical Design Authority (TDA) is the technical decision-making authority. It agrees roadmaps, and grants authority to solution design authorities.
  • In a solution design authority, the principal architect is accountable for decisions, as long as they align with a roadmap agreed at the TDA, follow the architecture principles and work within the guardrails.

A decision that would not align with the agreed roadmap, or would go outside the guardrails, goes to the TDA.

docs.title: Delivery partners and SDAs
docs.text: Partner architects often present to and contribute to SDAs. The decision, though, sits with the principal architect accountable for the SDA. Partners should expect their designs to be assessed against these guardrails and should record decisions as ADRs in Defra repositories.

docs.title: Terms of reference outline
docs.text:
• Scope: services, products and business capabilities covered
  • Membership: principal architect (chair), architects from the group, a security architect, a data architect, platform representative; product and delivery leads as needed
  • Delegated authority: decisions it may make, with reference to this page
  • Escalation: to the TDA, following triage
  • Cadence: as needed, with a maximum 5-working-day turnaround for decisions
  • Transparency: ADR log location; quarterly summary to the TDA

docs.title: Technical Design Authority (TDA)
docs.text:
The TDA is Defra's technical decision-making authority. It agrees roadmaps, grants authority to solution design authorities, and reviews cross-cutting and novel work and exceptions to the guardrails. It is a peer review that helps teams get to a good design - not an exam.

Draft - to be confirmed

Parts of this page, such as names, timings and thresholds, are still being confirmed by the architecture team. Use it as a guide, and check with your solution design authority before relying on the detail.

docs.title: When to come to the TDA
docs.text:
Use which route do I take?. In short, come to the TDA when your work:

  • is novel for Defra - new technology, pattern or use of AI
  • is cross-cutting - other services, teams or arm's length bodies will depend on it or be affected by it
  • needs an exception to a Must guardrail
  • fills a gap in the technology capabilities
  • is escalated by a solution design authority

Come early. The best time is the end of discovery or early alpha, when changing direction is cheap. You can come more than once.

docs.title: What the TDA does
docs.text:
• Reviews designs and gives clear, actionable outcomes
  • Approves or declines time-limited exceptions to Must guardrails
  • Identifies reuse opportunities between teams
  • Feeds lessons into the guardrails and handrail
  • Recommends items to the TGB

docs.title: Membership
docs.text: Chaired by the Chief Architect or a delegate, with enterprise, solution, data and security architects, platform representatives and, for relevant items, arm's length body architects. Delivery partners presenting on behalf of a Defra team are welcome to attend.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Step What happens Timing 1. Talk to us An informal conversation with an architect to shape the submission Any time 2. Submit Complete the TDA submission template and email it with any ADRs and diagrams - see raise a decision for review 5 working days before the meeting 3. Review 30-minute slot: 10 minutes to present, 20 minutes discussion Fortnightly 4. Outcome Recorded in the architecture decision register and shared within 3 working days

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text: Outcome Means Endorsed Proceed. Endorsed with conditions Proceed, meeting named conditions by a named date. Not endorsed Rework and come back. The TDA explains why and offers support. Escalated The decision needs the TGB.

docs.title: What good looks like in a submission
docs.text:
• The problem and outcome in plain English, and the business capabilities affected
  • The options considered, including the strategic options from the handrail, and why you prefer one
  • A context diagram and a container-level diagram (the C4 model works well)
  • Which guardrails you meet and which you do not
  • Risks, including security (a current threat model) and data protection
  • What you need from the TDA - a decision, advice or an exception

Short is better. Five pages is plenty.

docs.title: Technology Governance Board (TGB)
docs.text:
The TGB sets Defra's technology direction. It approves strategies, standards and guardrails, and the investment that shapes Defra's technology estate.

Draft - to be confirmed

Parts of this page, such as names, timings and thresholds, are still being confirmed by the architecture team. Use it as a guide, and check with your solution design authority before relying on the detail.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The TGB ensures Defra's digital, data and technology estate supports departmental outcomes, is secure and sustainable, and represents value for money. It is where Defra decides what good looks like; the TDA and solution design authorities make sure it happens.

docs.title: What the TGB decides
docs.text:
• Digital, data and technology strategies and roadmaps
  • Architecture principles and Must guardrails
  • Adoption, change or retirement of strategic platforms and technology capabilities
  • Changes to level 1 business capabilities
  • Technology aspects of significant investment cases
  • Escalations from the TDA, including risks outside Defra's appetite

docs.title: What the TGB does not do
docs.text: It does not review individual service designs. Those are delegated to the TDA and solution design authorities.

docs.title: Membership
docs.text: Role Responsibility Chief Digital and Information Officer (chair) Accountable for decisions Chief Technology Officer / Chief Architect Architecture direction; owner of the guardrails Chief Information Security Officer Security risk Chief Data Officer Data strategy and standards Heads of digital delivery and platforms Delivery and operational impact Arm's length body technology leads Group-wide alignment Commercial and finance representatives Commercial and investment implications

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Meets monthly, with papers circulated a week in advance.
  • Items normally arrive via the TDA, which provides a recommendation.
  • Decisions, and the reasons for them, are recorded and published here where they are not sensitive.

docs.title: Bringing an item to the TGB
docs.text: Talk to the architecture team first. Most items need a short paper covering: the decision needed, options considered, recommendation, impact on the guardrails and handrail, cost, risk and the TDA's view.

docs.title: Which route do I take?
docs.text:
Answer five questions to find the lightest governance route that fits your work.

Prefer an interactive version?

The decision check walks you through these questions, suggests a route and drafts a decision record for you.

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Governance triage decision tree
    accDescr: Changes to strategy or strategic platforms go to the Technology Governance Board. Exceptions to Must guardrails, and novel or cross-cutting work, go to the Technical Design Authority. Departures from Should guardrails, phase gates and significant changes go to the solution design authority. Everything else is self-assured and recorded in an ADR.
    A([Start]) --> Q1{"Does it change Defra<br/>technology strategy, or<br/>create or retire a<br/>strategic platform?"}
    Q1 -->|Yes| TGB["Technology<br/>Governance Board"]
    Q1 -->|No| Q2{"Do you need an exception<br/>to a <b>Must</b> guardrail?"}
    Q2 -->|Yes| TDA["Technical Design<br/>Authority"]
    Q2 -->|No| Q3{"Is it novel for Defra, or<br/>does it affect services<br/>beyond your own?"}
    Q3 -->|Yes| TDA
    Q3 -->|No| Q4{"Do you depart from a<br/><b>Should</b> guardrail or a<br/>strategic capability?"}
    Q4 -->|Yes| SDA["Solution design<br/>authority"]
    Q4 -->|No| Q5{"Is it a phase gate<br/>or significant change?"}
    Q5 -->|Yes| SDA
    Q5 -->|No| SELF["Self-assure and<br/>record an ADR"]

docs.title: 1. Does it change strategy or a strategic platform?
docs.text: Examples: adopting a new cloud provider, introducing a new strategic platform, changing a Must guardrail, retiring a capability used across Defra. These go to the Technology Governance Board, normally after review by the TDA.

docs.title: 2. Do you need an exception to a Must guardrail?
docs.text: Examples: hosting outside the Core Delivery Platform, building your own sign-in, keeping code private. Go to the Technical Design Authority via the exception process.

docs.title: 3. Is it novel or cross-cutting?
docs.text: Novel means Defra has not done it before: a new technology, a new integration pattern, a first use of generative AI in a service. Cross-cutting means other services, teams or arm's length bodies will depend on it or be affected by it: a new shared API, a change to a shared data set, a new identity integration pattern. Go to the TDA.

docs.title: 4. Do you depart from a Should guardrail or strategic capability?
docs.text: Record your reasoning in an ADR and agree it with your solution design authority.

docs.title: 5. Is it a phase gate or significant change?
docs.text: Share your architecture, ADR log and threat model with your SDA ahead of alpha, beta and live assessments, and before significant changes.

docs.title: Otherwise - self-assure
docs.text: Use the 10-minute self-assurance checklist, record significant decisions as ADRs, and carry on.

docs.title: Not sure?
docs.text: Ask. The architecture team runs drop-in sessions for teams and delivery partners and will tell you the right route - usually in a single conversation. See the architecture team.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Lightweight templates for the most common architecture artefacts. Copy them into your repository and adapt as needed.

Template Use it when Architecture decision record You make a significant design decision TDA submission You are bringing work to the Technical Design Authority Guardrail exception request You cannot meet a Must guardrail Threat model You are threat modelling a service or change

Each template is plain Markdown so it can live in your repository next to your code. Select Edit this page at the top right of any template to see its source.

docs.title: Architecture decision record template
docs.text:
Save as docs/adr/NNNN-short-title.md in your repository.

- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Deciders: names or roles
- Decided by: team | SDA name | TDA | TGB
- Business capabilities: e.g. BC05 Issue licences and permits
- Technology capabilities: e.g. TC08 Case and workflow management
- Guardrails: e.g. GR-HOST-01 (met), GR-DEV-01 (departure - see below)
- Advice sought from: e.g. platform team, security architect, teams affected

## Context

What is the problem or opportunity? What constraints and forces are at play
(user needs, policy, deadlines, existing systems, skills, cost)? Write for someone
who was not in the room.

## Options considered

## Consequences

- What becomes harder, or what risks are we accepting?
- What will we need to do as a result (follow-up work, exceptions, monitoring)?
- Exit: how would we reverse this if we needed to?

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text: Guardrails are opinionated, good-practice defaults for designing, building and running services in Defra. They exist so teams can make good decisions quickly, without waiting for permission.

docs.title: Why guardrails
docs.text:
Defra delivers hundreds of services across the core department and its arm's length bodies. Without shared defaults, every team solves the same problems again - hosting, identity, logging, payments - at extra cost and risk. Guardrails:

  • speed teams up by answering common questions once
  • make governance lighter - a design that stays inside the guardrails can be self-assured and needs no board
  • make Defra easier to work with - delivery partners know what we expect before they start
  • reduce risk by building in security, accessibility, data protection and sustainability from the start

Guardrails are not a gate.

Not the same as business analysis guardrails

The business analysis guardrails in the Defra Digital Service Manual are a separate quality framework for business analysis work. The guardrails on this site are architecture guardrails. They are the road with the barriers at the edge: you can drive as fast as you like in the middle.

docs.title: What the guardrails apply to
docs.text:
The guardrails apply to digital services and products that Defra builds, buys or runs. Some, such as GR-IAM-02, name software as a service explicitly.

To be confirmed

TODO: which guardrails apply to commercial off-the-shelf products and to data and reporting platforms. The architecture guidance in the Defra Digital Service Manual says it may not apply to deploying commercial off-the-shelf software or building a data or reporting platform.

docs.title: Arm's length bodies
docs.text:
To be confirmed

TODO: whether the guardrails apply to Defra's arm's length bodies as well as the core department, and any differences by area. Each area page links here until its applicability is confirmed; record the answer in that page's applicability front matter.

docs.title: How to read a guardrail
docs.text:
Each guardrail has an identifier, a level, a short rationale and a way to show you meet it.

Level Means If you cannot meet it Must A requirement from law or mandatory government policy, a baseline security control, or a DDTS doctrine non-negotiable. We keep these few. You need an approved exception from the Technical Design Authority. Should The strong default. There may be good reasons to differ. Record why in an architecture decision record and share it with your solution design authority. Could Recommended good practice. No action needed, but we would like to know what worked better.

Identifiers (for example GR-HOST-01) are stable so they can be referenced in decision records, assessments, contracts and statements of work. We never renumber, rename or delete an identifier: a guardrail that is no longer needed is marked deprecated and points to its replacement.

Under each guardrail, Phases, evidence and status shows:

  • status - draft, endorsed by the Technology Governance Board, or deprecated
  • phases - when it applies: discovery, alpha, beta or live
  • evidence - what to show an assessor or your solution design authority to prove you meet it, phase by phase: in discovery the intent or constraint you identified, in alpha the design or plan, in beta what you built and tested, and in live how you operate and review it
  • led by - the roles that make sure the team meets it, such as content designer or technical architect - see guardrails by role
  • automated check - whether it can be checked by a tool, or needs a person
  • the Service Standard, Technology Code of Practice and Secure by Design points it helps you meet, and the DDTS doctrine it applies

The same data is published as guardrails.json for tools and dashboards.

docs.text:
Search them all in the guardrail library, or browse by area:

docs.title: Self-assure in 10 minutes
docs.text:
Use this checklist at the end of discovery, at each phase gate and before any significant change. If you can tick every box you are inside the guardrails and can proceed with your solution design authority.

  • The service maps to one or more business capabilities and we have checked the technology capabilities for something to reuse
  • We are hosting on a strategic platform (GR-HOST-01) or have an agreed exception
  • Code is in a Defra GitHub organisation and public unless there is a recorded reason (GR-OPEN-01)
  • We use the strategic identity services for customers and staff (GR-IAM-01, GR-IAM-02)
  • Our APIs are documented with OpenAPI or AsyncAPI (GR-API-02)
  • We know who owns each data set we create or use, and we use authoritative sources (GR-DATA-01, GR-DATA-02)
  • We have a current threat model (GR-SEC-02) and a DPIA where personal data is involved (GR-DATA-06)
  • Logs, metrics and alerts flow to the platform's observability tooling (GR-OPS-01)
  • The service meets WCAG 2.2 AA and uses the GOV.UK Design System (GR-FE-01, GR-FE-02)
  • Significant decisions are recorded as ADRs (GR-DEV-09)

Ticked every box? Great - carry on, and record it. Not sure, or found a gap? Use the decision check to find the right route.

docs.title: How guardrails change
docs.text:
Guardrails are owned by the architecture team, reviewed by the Technical Design Authority and approved by the Technology Governance Board. Anyone can propose a change:

  1. Open an issue or pull request in the repository describing the change and why.
  2. The architecture team triages it within two weeks.
  3. Minor clarifications are merged directly. New or changed Must guardrails go to the TDA for review and to the TGB for approval.
  4. Changes are listed in what's new.

Repeated exceptions are a signal

If several teams need the same exception, the guardrail is probably wrong. We review exceptions every quarter and change guardrails when they get in the way.

docs.title: Artificial intelligence
docs.text:
AI can help Defra do more with less - from classifying species in images to drafting responses. These guardrails help teams use it safely, lawfully and transparently.

Doctrine: 4. Data is an enterprise asset, 5. Assume AI until proven otherwise Principles: 7. Empower to innovate, 4. Clean data, clear decisions

Who these guardrails apply to

The core department. Whether the artificial intelligence guardrails also apply to Defra's arm's length bodies is still to be confirmed.

Applies the DDTS doctrine assume AI until proven otherwise, and builds on the AI Playbook for the UK Government.

For practical guidance - which tools teams use, what data you can put into them, keeping data safe, working with AI agents and reporting an AI incident - use the AI digital toolkit in the Defra Digital Service Manual, run by the AI Capability and Enablement (AICE) team. Contact details for AICE are on the toolkit's home page. These guardrails set the architecture boundaries; the toolkit tells you how. Technology capability TC20 Artificial intelligence and machine learning.

docs.title: GR-AI-01 Consider AI first
docs.text:
Should When designing a service or process, actively explore whether AI can improve quality, productivity, user experience or outcomes before choosing a traditional approach, and record the reasoning either way.

Why: the DDTS doctrine says assume AI until proven otherwise. That does not mean AI everywhere; it means deliberately considering the opportunity before dismissing it.

How to meet it: in discovery and alpha, look for repetitive tasks, triage, summarising, classification or decision support that AI could help with. Note in your ADR what you considered and why you did or did not use AI.

In the AI digital toolkit: start with check if AI is right for your idea, five questions about the problem, users, data, benefits and what you have tried.

docs.title: GR-AI-02 Use approved AI services and tenancies
docs.text:
Must Services you build run their AI in Defra's cloud tenancies or under approved enterprise agreements. When anyone uses an AI tool, they put Defra data into it only as the using data with AI rules in the AI digital toolkit allow - for example, never OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or personal data in a public consumer tool.

In the AI digital toolkit: choosing a tool and keeping data safe.

docs.title: GR-AI-05 Evaluate, monitor and threat model
docs.text:
Should Evaluate models for accuracy, bias and safety before release, monitor them in live, and include AI-specific threats (prompt injection, data leakage, model abuse) in your threat model.

Cross-government AI tools

OCTO's AI technology enablement resources include an AI risk management toolkit, an AI assurance questionnaire, the public sector AI governance operating model and a service assessment questions navigator. Use them to evidence GR-AI-03, GR-AI-04 and GR-AI-05.

  • Beta: Evaluation results for accuracy, bias and safety before release, and mitigations for AI threats tested
  • Live: Monitoring of model performance and drift in live, with evaluation repeated when the model or data changes

docs.title: GR-AI-06 Talk to the TDA about novel use
docs.text:
Should Novel uses of AI, and any use of generative AI in decision making, are reviewed by the Technical Design Authority.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-06StatusDraftPhasesDiscovery, AlphaLed byTechnical architectEvidence
  • Discovery: Novel or generative AI use in decision making identified, and a conversation with the Technical Design Authority booked
  • Alpha: Technical Design Authority review outcome recorded in the ADR
  • Significant change: Technical Design Authority review of any new AI use introduced by the change
Automated checkManualDDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-AI-07 Suppliers use AI coding assistants openly and safely
docs.text:
Should Delivery partners who use AI coding assistants on Defra work agree which tools they use with Defra, use them only under terms that meet GR-AI-02, have a person review every change before it is merged, and say in pull requests or delivery reports where AI did significant work.

Why: AI coding assistants can speed up delivery, but they can also leak code, secrets or data to a third party, bring in code with unclear licences, and produce plausible but wrong code. Defra owns the code it pays for and must be able to trust it.

How to meet it:

  • Follow choosing a tool and using data with AI in the AI digital toolkit: what matters is the data you put in, and privacy settings must be on.
  • Tell the Defra engagement lead which tools you use at mobilisation, and record them in the repository.
  • Follow AI security in the AI digital toolkit: AI-written code clears the same Defra security gates as any other code.
  • Never put secrets into prompts.
  • Review AI-generated code with the same care as any other code (GR-DEV-03), including licences of any suggested code.

This guardrail is a draft proposal. Comment on it by opening an issue.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-07StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed byDelivery manager, DeveloperEvidenceSupplier's agreed list of AI coding assistants and how each runs within Defra-approved terms, the review process for generated code, and disclosure in pull requests or delivery reportsAutomated checkManualMaps toSecure by Design principles 2, 10DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.2.0

docs.title: Agentic AI
docs.text: AI agents do more than answer questions: they plan steps and take actions through tools, such as updating records, sending messages or calling APIs. That makes them useful, and it makes mistakes and attacks more costly. For how to build agents in Defra - identity, connecting tools, evaluations and tracing, and which platforms are ready - see working with AI agents in the AI digital toolkit, and talk to AICE before you choose a platform. These draft guardrails come from the guardrail backlog and apply on top of GR-AI-02 to GR-AI-06.

docs.title: GR-AI-08 Give agents the least privilege they need
docs.text:
Should AI agents act under their own identity, with access only to the tools, data and actions their task needs, and never with a person's full permissions.

Why: an agent can be tricked, or can be wrong. Limiting what it can reach limits the damage (GR-IAM-03).

How to meet it: list each agent's tools and permissions, grant them to a workload identity for the agent, and review them as you would a privileged user's.

In the AI digital toolkit: working with AI agents.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-08StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed byTechnical architect, Security architectEvidence
  • Alpha: Each agent's tools and permissions listed in the design, with a workload identity for the agent
  • Beta: Agent permissions configured as designed and tested, including that the agent cannot reach tools it should not
  • Live: Agent permissions reviewed regularly, as for a privileged user
Automated checkManualMaps toSecure by Design principles 7DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.2.0

docs.title: GR-AI-09 Get human approval for consequential actions
docs.text:
Should An agent does not take an action with legal, financial or significant effects on people, or one that cannot easily be undone, without approval from an accountable person.

Why: GR-AI-03 keeps a human accountable for decisions. Agents act faster than people can notice, so approval has to be designed in, not assumed.

How to meet it: classify the agent's actions in alpha. Enforce approval in the tool layer, not only in the prompt, and test that the agent cannot bypass it.

In the AI digital toolkit: working with AI agents.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-09StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed byService designer, Technical architectEvidence
  • Alpha: Agent actions classified, and the actions that need human approval identified in the design
  • Beta: Approval enforced in the tool layer, with tests showing the agent cannot act without it
  • Live: Approval records reviewed, and the classification updated when the agent gains new tools
Automated checkManualMaps toSecure by Design principles 4DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.2.0

docs.title: GR-AI-10 Keep an audit trail of what agents do
docs.text:
Should Record what each agent was asked, what it read, which tools it called with what inputs, who approved what, and the outcome - and send security-relevant events to security monitoring.

Why: without a full record, nobody can explain, challenge or reverse what an agent did.

How to meet it: log at the tool layer with correlation ids (GR-OPS-02), and keep records for as long as the decisions they support.

In the AI digital toolkit: working with AI agents.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-10StatusDraftPhasesBeta, LiveLed byDeveloper, Security architectEvidence
  • Beta: Audit records of agent inputs, tool calls, approvals and outcomes produced and sent to security monitoring
  • Live: Audit records retained and reviewed, and used to investigate any problem
Automated checkManualMaps toSecure by Design principles 5DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.2.0

docs.title: GR-AI-11 Defend agents against prompt injection
docs.text:
Should Treat everything an agent reads - documents, emails, web pages, tool results - as untrusted input that may try to change its instructions, and design controls that hold even if it does.

Why: prompt injection is the most common way to make an agent misuse its tools or leak data.

How to meet it: include injection through every input in your threat model (GR-AI-05), separate untrusted content from instructions, restrict tools as in GR-AI-08 and require approval as in GR-AI-09.

In the AI digital toolkit: working with AI agents.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-AI-11StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed bySecurity architect, DeveloperEvidence
  • Alpha: Threat model covering prompt injection through every input the agent reads
  • Beta: Prompt injection mitigations tested, including attempts to misuse tools and leak data
  • Live: Prompt injection defences re-tested when inputs, tools or models change
Automated checkManualMaps toSecure by Design principles 3, 8DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.2.0

docs.title: APIs and integration
docs.text:
How services talk to each other and to partners. Good integration lets us reuse capabilities and change one part of Defra without breaking another.

Doctrine: 4. Data is an enterprise asset, 6. Outcomes and services over organisational structures Principles: 5. Connect and collaborate

Who these guardrails apply to

The core department. Whether the APIs and integration guardrails also apply to Defra's arm's length bodies is still to be confirmed.

Technology capability TC22 API management and integration.

docs.title: GR-API-01 API first
docs.text:
Should Design the API for a capability before (or with) the user interface, so other services and partners can use it.

docs.title: GR-API-02 Describe APIs with open specifications

Should Synchronous APIs are described with OpenAPI 3, and asynchronous/event interfaces with AsyncAPI, kept in the same repository as the code.

docs.title: GR-API-03 Follow government API standards
docs.text:
Should Follow the API technical and data standards: RESTful resources, JSON, HTTPS only, consistent error formats and standard identifiers from the data standards.

docs.title: GR-API-04 Version and deprecate deliberately
docs.text:
Should Breaking changes are versioned, consumers are told in advance, and old versions have a published retirement date.

docs.title: GR-API-05 No integration through shared databases
docs.text:
Should Services do not read or write another service's database directly. Integrate through APIs, events or governed data products.

Why: Shared databases tightly couple services and make both impossible to change safely.

docs.title: GR-API-06 Use events for change notifications
docs.text:
Should Use asynchronous messages or events when other services need to react to something that happened (an application submitted, a permit issued), rather than polling.

docs.title: GR-API-07 Secure every API
docs.text:
Must All APIs authenticate callers (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect or mutual TLS), authorise every request, validate input and apply rate limiting. No API is "internal so it's safe".

docs.text:
Should Register APIs in the platform API catalogue and, where they are useful beyond Defra, the government API catalogue.

docs.title: Choosing technology
docs.text:
How to decide whether to reuse, buy or build - and how to avoid being stuck with the choice.

Doctrine: 1. Platforms before projects. Built as products, 2. Standards and guardrails before exceptions, 3. Reuse before buy Principles: 3. Maximise value, minimise waste, 1. Delivery-focused architecture

Who these guardrails apply to

The core department. Whether the choosing technology guardrails also apply to Defra's arm's length bodies is still to be confirmed.

docs.title: GR-TECH-01 Look for something to reuse first
docs.text:
Must Before buying or building, check the technology capability catalogue and cross-government components for something that already meets the need.

Why: Duplicate capabilities multiply cost, security risk and support effort.

How to meet it: Record in your ADR which strategic options you considered and why they did or did not fit. If a strategic option is close but not quite right, talk to the owning platform team before building around it.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-TECH-01StatusDraftPhasesDiscovery, AlphaLed byTechnical architectEvidence
  • Discovery: Existing Defra and cross-government options for the need identified from the technology capability catalogue
  • Alpha: ADR recording the reuse options considered and why they did or did not fit
  • Significant change: ADR showing reuse options considered for any new component
Automated checkManualMaps toService Standard 13; Technology Code of Practice 8DDTS doctrine1, 2, 3OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-TECH-02 Buy commodity, build differentiating
docs.text:
Should Buy or use SaaS for commodity needs (email, HR, finance, CRM, document management). Build only where the capability is specific to Defra's mission and no product fits without heavy customisation.

Why: Heavily customised products combine the cost of building with the constraints of buying.

How to meet it: If you are configuring more than you are using out of the box, stop and reconsider. Prefer configuration over customisation; avoid modifying vendor code.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-TECH-02StatusDraftPhasesDiscovery, AlphaLed byTechnical architect, Product managerEvidenceBuy or build options appraisal in the ADR or business caseAutomated checkManualMaps toService Standard 11; Technology Code of Practice 11DDTS doctrine1, 2, 3OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-TECH-03 Plan your exit before you enter
docs.text:
Should Any new product, platform or significant supplier dependency has a documented exit plan covering data export in open formats, contract terms and an estimate of switching cost.

Why: Lock-in is sometimes a sensible trade-off, but it must be a deliberate one.

How to meet it: Include an exit section in your ADR or business case. Make sure contracts give Defra ownership of its data and the right to export it.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-TECH-03StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed byTechnical architect, Delivery managerEvidence
  • Alpha: Draft exit plan for each new product, platform or significant supplier
  • Beta: Exit plan agreed, with contracts giving Defra its data and the right to export it in open formats
  • Live: Exit plan reviewed at contract renewal, with switching cost estimated
  • Significant change: Exit plan updated for any new product or supplier
  • Retire: Exit plan carried out - data exported in open formats and contracts ended
Automated checkManualMaps toTechnology Code of Practice 11DDTS doctrine1, 2, 3OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-TECH-04 Assess SaaS before you adopt it
docs.text:
Must SaaS and third-party hosted products are assessed for security, data protection, data location, accessibility and integration before contract.

Why: Supply chain risk is one of the biggest sources of security incidents in government.

How to meet it: Use the Secure by Design supplier assurance activities, complete a DPIA if personal data is involved and confirm the product supports single sign-on with Microsoft Entra ID for staff (GR-IAM-02).

  • Alpha: Security, data protection, data location, accessibility and single sign-on assessed before contract
Automated checkManualMaps toService Standard 9; Technology Code of Practice 6, 7, 11; Secure by Design principles 2DDTS doctrine1, 2, 3OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-TECH-05 Prefer open standards and portable technology
docs.text:
Should Choose products and components that use open standards and can be run on more than one provider.

Why: Portability keeps our options open and our commercial position strong.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-TECH-05StatusDraftPhasesAlphaLed byTechnical architectEvidenceADR noting the open standards used and how portable the choice isAutomated checkManualMaps toService Standard 13; Technology Code of Practice 4DDTS doctrine1, 2, 3OwnerArchitecture team, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-TECH-06 Get spend approval early
docs.text:
Must Spend that falls under the government digital and technology spend control is discussed with the architecture team before procurement starts.

Why: Architecture questions raised at the end of a procurement are expensive to answer.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-TECH-06StatusDraftPhasesDiscoveryLed byDelivery manager, Product managerEvidence

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Defra's science, regulation and payments all depend on trusted data. These guardrails make sure the data each service creates is an asset for the whole department.

Doctrine: 4. Data is an enterprise asset, 5. Assume AI until proven otherwise Principles: 4. Clean data, clear decisions

Who these guardrails apply to

The core department. Whether the data guardrails also apply to Defra's arm's length bodies is still to be confirmed.

See also enterprise data architecture.

docs.title: GR-DATA-01 Every data set has an owner
docs.text:
Should Each data set a service creates or holds has a named business owner (information asset owner) and is recorded in the information asset register.

Why: Data without an owner is not maintained, not trusted and not deleted when it should be.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-DATA-01StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, Beta, LiveLed byData architect, Product managerEvidence
  • Alpha: Each data set the service will create or hold identified, with a proposed information asset owner
  • Beta: Information asset register entries with a named owner for each data set
  • Live: Register entries and owners kept current
  • Retire: Information asset register updated to show what happened to each data set
Automated checkManualMaps toTechnology Code of Practice 10DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerEnterprise data architecture, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-DATA-02 Use authoritative sources
docs.text:
Should Use the authoritative source for shared entities - customers, organisations, land parcels, holdings, locations, species - rather than creating local copies that drift. See Defra on a page.

How to meet it: If you must cache or replicate, record the source, refresh frequency and how you handle changes.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-DATA-02StatusDraftPhasesDiscovery, Alpha, Beta, LiveLed byData architectEvidence
  • Discovery: Shared entities the service needs identified, with their authoritative sources
  • Alpha: Data flow diagram naming the authoritative source for each shared entity, and how any copies are refreshed
  • Beta: The service reads from the authoritative sources as designed, tested with the source owners
  • Live: Copies and refresh arrangements reviewed when sources change
Automated checkManualMaps toTechnology Code of Practice 10DDTS doctrine4, 5OwnerEnterprise data architecture, last reviewed 2026-10-01, since v0.1.0

docs.title: GR-DATA-03 Use agreed data standards and identifiers
docs.text:
Should Use the data standards for dates, addresses, locations, identifiers and code lists, so data can be joined across services.

Phases, evidence and status for GR-DATA-03StatusDraftPhasesAlpha, BetaLed byData architectEvidence

  • Beta: Data stored and exchanged using the agreed standards, checked in testing

docs.title: GR-DATA-04 Collect once, share safely
docs.text:
Should Do not ask users for information Defra already holds. Share data between services through APIs or governed data products, with data sharing agreements where required.

docs.title: GR-DATA-05 Describe your data
docs.text:
Should Publish metadata for data sets so they can be found and understood - UK GEMINI for geospatial data and DCAT for other data sets.

docs.title: GR-DATA-06 Protect personal data by design
docs.text:
Must Complete a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before processing personal data, minimise what you collect, and apply retention and deletion automatically.

Why: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018; TCoP point 7.

docs.title: GR-DATA-07 Open by default
docs.text:
Should Publish non-personal, non-sensitive data as open data under the Open Government Licence, through the Defra Data Services Platform or data.gov.uk.

docs.title: GR-DATA-08 Manage data quality
docs.text:
Should Define, measure and report data quality using the Government Data Quality Framework, especially for data that feeds payments, regulatory decisions or official statistics.

docs.title: GR-DATA-09 Retain and dispose of records properly
docs.text:
Must Apply Defra's retention schedules. Records of permanent value are identified for transfer to The National Archives.
